o: Mountain i (for i ≥ 1) is stable exactly when height[i−1] > threshold; mountain 0 is never stable. For [1,2,3,4,5], threshold 2: mountains 3 and 4 have predecessors 3 and 4, both above 2. With n ≤ 100 a single linear scan is all that is required — constraints rule out any need for anything cleverer.
k: Stability of mountain i depends only on height[i−1] versus threshold — a purely local condition.
Index 0 is never stable, so the scan starts at index 1.

a.i: Walk from index 1 to n−1, comparing each predecessor against the threshold and collecting matches.
s: If height[i−1] > threshold, append i to the result.
a.sp: O(1) extra besides the output list.

a.i: The same condition expressed as a filtered comprehension / stream, which interviewers often like for brevity.
s: Pair each index i ≥ 1 with the test height[i−1] > threshold.
Collect and return the passing indices.
a.t: O(n) — same single pass, expressed declaratively.

w: Either version is fine; state the strict inequality (> threshold, not ≥) explicitly since that is the only real trap. Edge cases: no stable mountains (empty list), all mountains stable. Follow-up: what if stability depended on all previous mountains — that would become a prefix-maximum scan.
